extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and amateur scientists (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form popular-science magazine content explaining scientific concepts, reporting exploration/geography topics, biographical sketches of scientists, and opinion/correspondence on educational policy. Aimed at communicating science and scholarly topics to a general educated readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly qualifications for anthropological and linguistic research
rubrics_metrics.description: "To make such researches successful, one must of course be an accomplished scholar in Oriental linguistics and philosophy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an explicit prerequisite for successful anthropological/linguistic investigations among heterogeneous populations in western China and southwestern provinces. Implies projects of this kind require deep language and philosophical scholarship rather than purely exploratory travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical exploration desiderata (priority regions to investigate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists regions and specific geographic questions presented as desirable exploration targets: "the sources of the Hoang-Ho"; whether the Gobi is crossed by a chain of mountains connecting Thian-Shan with In-shan; the geological/mineral/zoological/botanical riches of the Kingan range; southwestern provinces of China and Indo-China (origins of immense rivers); Japan and Pacific archipelagoes; Afghanistan and Beloochistan; southern parts of Turkistan and the Oasis of Merv; discovery of ancient beds of the Oxus and its affluents; southern and interior Persia; parts of Arabia; Mesopotamia and Syria; Asia Minor and Armenia; examination of the Hellespont and Bosporus currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as concrete priorities/desiderata for scientific exploration and mapping — explicit targets and research questions that would advance geographical and natural-history knowledge. The text also notes some regions are better explored (British India) and others less so, guiding selection of future expeditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation over speculative cartography
rubrics_metrics.description: "Consequently, our maps of China are filled with chains of hypothetical mountains, which certain famous savants would like to impose upon us as the last word of modern science. Unfortunately for them, Nature has the bad habit of not agreeing with systems that are too learned…"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion advising skepticism of purely theoretical or learned map features without field verification. Maps and large-scale geographic assertions should be empirically confirmed by explorers/naturalists rather than accepted because they fit elegant systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power as the test of the molecular hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: "The theory that matter is built up of molecules depends... on its competence to explain observed facts. These are of two kinds — namely, physical and chemical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The molecular hypothesis should be judged by its ability to account for both physical phenomena (Boyle's law, Charles's law, gas pressure & molecular motion, diffusion) and chemical phenomena (law of definite proportions, atomic theory). Agreement between independent physical and chemical lines of evidence is presented as strong support — e.g., molecular weights deduced from gas behaviour agree with chemists' combining-proportion inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for determining molecular weights and velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of empirical methods: derive molecular velocities from measured gas pressure and estimated molecular mass (e.g., velocity of hydrogen molecule ~ six thousand feet/sec); use Avogadro's law and specific gravity of vapors relative to hydrogen to determine relative molecular weights: "The molecular weight of any substance... is found by simply determining experimentally the specific gravity of its vapor relatively to hydrogen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides how physicists/chemists ascertain molecular properties: apply gas laws (Boyle, Charles), measure vapor densities, use Avogadro's principle (equal gas volumes contain same number of molecules) and compare with chemical combining-proportions to obtain consistent relative molecular weights and velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for distinction in astronomy (qualities and accomplishments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit evaluative criteria drawn from the sketch of James Craig Watson: exceptional mathematical genius and intuition; rapid and accurate computation; mechanical tact and instrument construction; observational skill (discovery of comets, planets, minor planets); prolific and authoritative publication record (papers, treatises, textbooks); leadership in organized expeditions (eclipse and transit observations); original synthesis and development of theoretical principles (major treatise accepted as authoritative); practical contributions (actuarial work, institutional leadership, innovations in observatory design); honors and recognition by scientific societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a composite rubric for assessing an astronomer's eminence: combination of theoretical originality, observational discoveries, instrument skill, published influence (textbooks/reports), successful expedition leadership, and peer recognition (academy memberships, medals, degrees). The biography provides concrete examples (planetary discoveries, authoritative treatise, government expeditions) as evidentiary markers of distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of student self-government in colleges
rubrics_metrics.description: Described institutional principles: students permitted "perfect freedom in the election of courses of study"; discarding the "system of espionage" between faculty and students; recognizing the student's responsibility as an adult; imposing no trammels beyond obligation to respect others' rights; consequences are primarily personal (failure only harms the student); private admonition by the chairman or advice to leave, with the publicity of expulsion usually avoided; occasional students' court with no conflict with faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a policy rubric for organizing collegiate self-government: maximize student freedom of course choice; minimize surveillance; treat students as responsible adults; prefer private correction over public punishment; use student courts and avoid public expulsions when possible. Cited historical examples (University of Virginia, University of South Carolina) serve as applied evidence of the model's success.
